newsitem.title: UK: Strong pound gives helping hand to UK government.
newsitem.headline: Strong pound gives helping hand to UK government.

text.p: Four years after its humiliating exit from Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) the pound is back with a vengeance, giving the British government a weapon to fend off interest rate rises before the election, analysts said on Wednesday.
The pound has climbed over the past half a year to within a whisker of 2.7780 marks, the level from where it was ejected from the ERM on Black Wednesday in September 1992.

Its ERM exit was one of the most embarrassing political climbdowns in recent British history. But sterlings recovery is now helping the government, and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, to present voters with the sweetener of steady, and relatively low interest rates.
The strong comeback of the pound after it left the ERM is now allowing the chancellor to avoid a rise in interest rates, said Charles Goodhart, professor at the London School of Economics.
Politically this is a plus since he can avoid doing something that would be potentially negative ahead of an election, he said.
Sterlings strength is deemed by Clarke as sufficient to suppress inflationary forces after the pounds increase of about 14 percent on a trade-weighted basis in the past six months.
The steep climb has given Clarke a reason to resist calls for interest rate rises from Bank of England (BOE) Governor Eddie George.
Some economists question the economic wisdom of keeping rates on hold until after the election but for the British electorate the longer-term implications of monetary policy are less of a worry.

Interest rates and what they do to the pound in your pocket are a main concern for this nation of home-owners. A rise so close to the election, which must be held by May 1997, would hit the already unpopular Conservative Party even further as mortgages increase.
The drawback of a strong pound has been highlighted lately by British exporters saying its strength was eating away at their earnings.

The inflation-conscious Bank of England conceded on Wednesday that sterlings strength would lead to a drop in inflation for about 12 months as import prices fell, even though it maintained its call for a rate rise now.
Low inflation and a strong pound give the government the best of both worlds, although it might not be enough to win the election, analysts said.
Its a pretty good picture for Clarke that allows him to sit back until after the election, said Tim Fox, economist at Standard Chartered in London
For the electorate, the strong pound means more spending power abroad and the psychological effect of a strong currency might also contribute to the feel good factor.
There is slightly irrational pride in having an appreciating currency, which links a strong currency to a strong nation, said Goodhart.
The firm pound might also help to repair some of the damage done to the governments reputation for economic competence after the pounds ERM exit.

Four years ago the governments stated policy was to keep the pound in the exchange rate mechanism, and once the main plank of that strategy collapsed, its competence was being impaired, said Goodhart.
The contradictions surrounding sterlings withdrawal from the ERM are still a major influence on how the public views the Conservatives economic judgement.
Just days before the pound left the ERM, Majors government had vowed to keep sterling as part of Europes strong currency club along with the mark.
Major viewed ERM membership as the centrepiece of his economic strategy and vowed never to devalue.

Even as British interest rates had to be raised twice in a day to defend the pound against speculative attacks in September 1992, Norman Lamont, then chancellor, said Britain would take whatever measures necessary to keep sterling in the ERM.

Only a few days later, and after spending more than a quarter of Britains foreign exchange reserves to defend sterling against speculators, the government lauded a weaker pound as good for Britain, and advocated the potential gains for British industry of a weaker currency.

But wide-ranging economic reforms, such as increased flexibility in the labour market and increased investment in Britain, have helped to improve the governments economic standing, analysts said. -- London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
